Quiz 3

Amanda Mae Woodward

2025-10-30

  1. Load the spotify dataset (available in github repository).
library(tidyverse)
## ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
## ✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
## ✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
## ✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
## ✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
## ✔ purrr     1.2.2     
## ── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
## ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
## ✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
## ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors
spotify <- read_csv("spotifyDat Fall26.csv")
## Rows: 2000 Columns: 6
## ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## Delimiter: ","
## chr (3): artist, song, genre
## dbl (3): popularity, danceability, tempo
## 
## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
  1. Create a bar graph of the artist column (Hint: use theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90)) to rotate the x axis).
ggplot(spotify, aes(artist)) +geom_bar()+theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle=90))

  1. Add genre as a third variable in your graph.
ggplot(spotify, aes(artist, fill = genre)) + geom_bar() + theme(axis.title.x = element_text(angle = 90))

  1. Use color brewer to add color to your graph in 3.
ggplot(spotify, aes(artist, fill=genre)) +geom_bar()+scale_fill_brewer(palette="Set3")+ theme(axis.title.x = element_text(angle = 90))
## Warning in RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(n, pal): n too large, allowed maximum for palette Set3 is 12
## Returning the palette you asked for with that many colors

  1. Place the legend for the graph you made in 3 on the bottom of the graph.
ggplot(spotify, aes(artist, fill=genre)) +geom_bar()+scale_fill_brewer(palette="Set3")+ theme(axis.title.x = element_text(angle = 90))+ theme(legend.position="bottom")
## Warning in RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(n, pal): n too large, allowed maximum for palette Set3 is 12
## Returning the palette you asked for with that many colors

As you probably recognized, the graph you made is really hard to read. 6. Separate the genre column into multiple columns (e.g. so each genre listed is in a unique column)

spotify2 <- spotify |>
  separate(genre, into = c("genre1", "genre2", "genre3", "genre4"), sep=",", fill = "right")
  1. Use these genre columns to create a dataset in long format.
spotify3 <- spotify2 |>
  pivot_longer(cols = genre1:genre4, names_to ="genre_number", values_to="genre", values_drop_na=TRUE)

8.use facet wrap to make graphs of artist by genre

ggplot(spotify3, aes(artist))+ geom_bar()+ facet_wrap(~genre)+theme(axis.title.x = element_text(angle = 90))

  1. Create a graph that includes the variables tempo and dancability.
ggplot(spotify, aes(tempo, danceability))+ geom_point()

  1. Add popularity as a third variable.
ggplot(spotify, aes(tempo, danceability, color= popularity))+ geom_point()

  1. Use viridis as a color in your graph from #10
library(viridis)
## Loading required package: viridisLite
ggplot(spotify, aes(tempo, danceability, color= popularity))+ geom_point()+scale_color_viridis(discrete = FALSE, option = "magma")
